findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for, and why it matters, in plain words. They could repeat it after one read.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable.

findings.text: The page explains up front that what follows is an example of Athena's output about a different project. Without this, a reader who came for Athena would be confused to find the page is mostly about firstmate.
findings.source: A study is Athena's written reading of another software project, taken at one fixed commit ... This page is that study of firstmate.

findings.text: There is a link near the top that jumps to concrete next steps. The Next steps section lists prerequisites, the clone command, ./setup.sh and a sample `athena ask` command, so the reader knows how to try it.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

findings.text: This link sits in the header next to the newcomer's next step, but it is meant for the project owner. A first-time reader cannot tell whether it applies to them.
findings.source: Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision.

findings.text: Almost all of the page is detailed firstmate internals: 11 transition cards, 6 design cards and 44 claims. A newcomer who wants to judge Athena has to infer its value from how rigorous this example is, and the page never says which parts are worth skimming.
findings.source: States of a piece of work / Counters / Transitions / Claims and sources

findings.text: The Counters section points to transition ids before the Transitions section has defined them, so a reader reading top to bottom meets t1–t11 as unexplained labels.
findings.source: places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11

findings.text: Several terms are used but never defined for an outsider: "wake", "endpoint", "durable record", "delivery mode" and "captain-held inventory". The glossary entry for stale wake relies on "wake", which it does not explain.
findings.source: stale wake: A wake after which the agent inspects a worker that may have stopped, looped or gone quiet.

findings.text: This sentence about where to find the decider definitions is awkward. The definitions actually come right after the paragraph, before the cards.
findings.source: The two deciders are explained below the cards' heading.

findings.text: The glossary calls Done "the final state", but the States section says Reopened also ends the task. That is a small inconsistency a careful newcomer could trip on.
findings.source: done: The final state: the task record is removed and the backlog close has landed.

findings.text: The About this page section refers to a studies/ folder without saying which repository it is in. A newcomer has no context for it.
findings.source: This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from.
